utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic to continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We left off yesterday with you explaining the pressure that was put on Albanian civilians by the KLA. You opened tab 138. Could you give us a brief explanation now about the contents. Just let us go very briefly through these things.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, we started quoting yesterday from this page 3 in the Serbian version, which is marked 2/346/98. This is in fact the translation of a letter that KLA members sent to one of their fellow villagers, putting pressure on him to leave something for them in a certain spot because he had allegedly failed to comply with their earlier demands. The text begins with this sentence: "We have concluded that you are ignoring our appeal!!!" The second part of the text - we read the first yesterday - goes: "The staff orders you to extend assistance to our units at risk - otherwise you are in trouble. At 1930 hours on Thursday, 20 August, 1998, you will park your Passat car in the Famipa factory parking lot. The vehicle is to be unlocked, leave the keys in the vehicle and 5.000 Deutschmark on the driver's seat; leave your pistol on the other seat. We know whom you took it from and why. If you do not hand it over, men from SUP will come and confiscate it although Cerim has a buddy in SUP, but this time luck won't be on his side." Paragraph 4: "We in the KLA are involved in the abduction, maltreatment and disappearance of several people, so don't be surprised!!!" Next paragraph: "Do not get into a situation where you could be liquidated!!! "Do not forget that we will pay you a visit at the end of the month to talk about --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Milosevic, just extract what you wish from it. This is not a reading class.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted us to see, since there are very few documents about maltreatment of Albanians by the KLA, because maltreatment is normally not accompanied by documentation. The reference here is to abductions and blackmail. I want us to see what actually happened, in which way they extorted money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This shows, General, that they are threatening the man with liquidation if he fails to comply with his demands -- with their demands. Is that what is written?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This just goes to illustrate one of my answers yesterday about the pressure put by the KLA on their own fellow citizens and villagers to donate vehicles, money, and other things for the needs of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this paper, 1/346, is also about demands, and it says they will not acknowledge any excuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're on these documents, which I'm just about managing to identify in the collection of B/C/S versions, might it be helpful to know what generation of original or copy we have here? If the witness has brought the originals and if in due course the document becomes an exhibit, then the original should become an exhibit, and I'd quite like to have a look at it sooner rather than later. If we are only being provided with copies, perhaps that can be made clear, with an explanation of where the original may be found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask the witness. Is this -- General, do you have the original, the original version of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not in possession of the original, Your Honours. In my tab I have a copy of these documents. But I'm absolutely certain that the original of this document exists in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Documents like this here, is that not an original document? He's headed -- it's on paper that's headed "Grafix Impex."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course this is obviously a copy of the original, a photocopy of the original which was written on the agenda issued by a company, and the text is handwritten. All I wanted to say is that I don't have literally the original of the document. I don't know whether we interpret the concept of "original" in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And could you remind me where this was found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was found after one anti-terrorist action, if I remember correctly. And it is written on this first page in the village of Leskovac, in the Prizren municipality, on the 3rd of September, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As for the document we just referred to, which was allegedly written by KLA, do you have any idea how the Ministry of Interior was able to get the original copy of it? How did it come into possession of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I wasn't clear enough. This original document was found after one anti-terrorist action in the place which I already named in my previous answer, very close to the town of Prizren. So it was found after the anti-terrorist action was completed in this place, probably in one of the houses that had been used as headquarters or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But upon its face it is not clear by whom it is written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course you can view this document in that way as well, but its contents are self-evident. It is obviously written by a member of the KLA because you can see that from the text itself and you can see what the purpose and the meaning of such messages is. This is a very large material. I just tried to quote from one of the pages. In the rest of this material you can see many other details speaking to the KLA, such as lists, rosters, et cetera. I quoted from this page in connection with the previous question which related to the pressure exerted by the KLA on their own fellow villagers, and I thought this page well illustrated my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: More correctly, it expresses sentiments that would reasonably be attributable to the KLA, but it doesn't say necessarily that it was written by a KLA person. The sentiments are those that one would ordinarily attribute to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, unless I'm mistaken in my attempt to sort the papers, this page, 2346/98, and the previous page, 1346/98, are the pages for which we have no translations in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour has them, then I've mislaid mine or I'm not following the papers correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember a one-page document was distributed in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've located it. Ms. Dicklich knew where it was all along. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There does seem to be a wider problem, though. My file of Serb documents is at least twice if not three times as thick as the English translation file, so it doesn't look as though we have translations of everything that's in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, as for this last question asked by Mr. Robinson, whether this is indeed the KLA, can we see from this document which you quoted, 2-346/98, this quotation: "We from the KLA..."?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that follows the warning: "Do not get into a situation where you could be liquidated!!!"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at the copy of the original with the handwriting in Albanian. You can see dates. And in this Serb -- Serbian translation, they begin with this 3/346 document and then follow other dates. Can you just quote some of the most characteristic features of this text.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read everything, but just for example, on the page which is marked 3-346/98, it looks like an entry in a diary or in an agenda, and we see an entry for the 17th of July. "Malic Shala was designated to go and pick up the weapons. His father did not allow him to go. Today on the 17th of July, he was taken to be interrogated together with his son Shalam [phoen]." We can also recognise here a sort of pressure on somebody to do something for the KLA. Umer and Agim wanted to join him and go there, and this other person says, "I don't have to go because I am not subject to recruitment. I am exempted." This document speaks to a number of other issues other than what we discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on that same page, after the line that was drawn, then we have document 4-346. It says -- the staff is mentioned, and it says: "The region of Has together with Djakovica asked to be linked up with the same -- with the latter because their staff is near Rogovo, the staff from Renovac [phoen]. In the meantime we worked with Petrocev's [phoen] staff."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the explanation is that Mustafa and Shukrija talked to the staff from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that they were interested in the way supplies were being organised.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does this document leave any doubt whatsoever, then, that it is talking about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the circumstances under which this document was found, as well as its contents and the contents of each of these documents, indisputably show that they are documents belonging to members of the KLA from this particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at document 4-346, two pages on, and the date is the 19th of July, 1998. And what is mentioned there -- or, rather, names are mentioned, and then it says, "Last night there were conflicts during the arrivals from Albania by persons who had taken up weapons."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Several of them were from the village of Vrbnica. The rest were from other villages. Everybody returned to Vrbnica whereas the fate of two of them is not known.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a topic we've already covered, and that is how weapons were illegally brought in from the Republic of Albania and the problems surrounding that as they saw it from their point of view. And then we can see that the conflict lasted from two to five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the last sentence says: "Of the 40 persons who took part in the fighting --" so there was a group of 40 KLA members who clashed at the border with organs of border security.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that something that we can see from this document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Of the 40 who fought, were able to flee --" and then we have a cut-off there, and after the dotted line on the next page, it says, "-- weapons in the forest, in the woods." Yes. I've been asked to make a pause between question and answer. So it said they left a quantity of weapons in the woods. The number of persons from whom weapons were confiscated is unknown. Then it goes on to explain about another group who crossed the border. It's about this group who crossed the border carrying weapons, and this group, when it crossed Vrbnica and the watchtower there, that there was fighting along the border and that the fighting went on from 0200 hours to 0330 hours. And then it says, "Half the village moved further away and the situation is insecure, unsafe."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that confirms our thesis about villagers and citizens moving away from the area they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Udaljavanja" that we discussed earlier on, about people moving away from, et cetera, et cetera. And then it says that half the inhabitants took refuge in Prizren, Zur, and other places. And then it says that 40 persons were armed. And then once again the next sentence it says in Dobok [phoen] about 40 persons were armed. And then the following sentence, that people in Muradem were partially armed. And then it talks about mortars and hand grenades and so on at the end of that page, 27. And shells. And it says that on the 20th of July, ten were sent and they were all carrying weapons, and then the question is who sent the people in the first place. That is to be found under the date 20th of July, 1998. All the rest of it refers to or, rather, names names of the members of the KLA who were being sent to certain locations. And then on the following page, it says: "Vrbnica, two people remained in Brezne." That is document 7-346/98. And then it goes to say -- on to say: "Of this number, there were 11 automatic rifles, three rifles, five" et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, is it your case that some of this evidence answers some of the allegations relating to the forced movement of people, deportation? This relates to 1998. I ask the question because one of the answers given by the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was, "That confirms our thesis about villagers and citizens moving away from the area they were in." So I'm seeking to find out whether you're adducing this evidence as an answer to any specific allegations in the indictment concerning the forced movement of people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly that is further proof. When the general said that this confirms the assertion that the population was fleeing from the area where the conflict was taking place, it is quite clear that it wasn't the police that were expelling them. Secondly, from this document, or from these documents, we can see that the groups, and here for example a group of 40 individuals crossing the border was mentioned. A group of armed persons crossing the border, crossing the border in this way, violently, were clashing with the army. So those groups and their conflict with the army of the neighbouring state causes armed conflict which have as their consequence the fleeing of the population. So there was no activity on the part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what about the time element? This is 1998, not 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, due to force of circumstance, these documents were seized, and they were seized at that time and referred to 1998. But the events were the same. What was happening was the same, because the population behaved the same. Where there were conflicts, the population fled. And how clashes and conflicts broke out you can see on the basis of this example. They were storming the border armed, they clashed with the army, and it says half the population fled to Prizren and Zur. The other half went somewhere else, in other directions. So this is the same sequence of events throughout the whole time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I could see that it would have that kind of evidential value as indicating a pattern, but I'm not sure whether it requires being dwelt on in this detail. I think you have shown that this kind -- let me finish. You have shown that this happened in 1998. You should move more quickly to 1999. I accept that there is a linkage, because the fact that it happened in 1998 would make it more credible, more believable that the same thing happened in 1999, on the basis of your case, but bring us to 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from this document -- of course everything that the general is testifying about refers to 1999 as well. Many of the areas covered refer to 1999. But if you look two pages on, it is the translation of document 12-115, dated the 31st of March, 1999, you have it there. So we're talking about 31st of March, 1999, and it says that the commander of the 2nd Battalion from Buda [phoen] decided to launch an attack on the Serbian village of Muhovljani where there were Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The heading for these documents says they were all found on the 3rd of September, 1998. So this must be a separate document from the ones that are in the bundle I've been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are still trying to find the -- your last reference to 1999, 31st of March, 1999. Mr. Kay, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found it, but it seems to be a separate document. 12-115.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12/ or -115/99. That's what I'm quoting. It's not from the diary, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we have no English translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, don't proceed yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, at this stage we'll not hear any more evidence relating to 1998. Move to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, do you have document 12-115/99 of the 31st of March, 1999, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it talk about the attack of the KLA on the village of Muhovljani where they say there are Serb forces located?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says in para 1. But in the one but last paragraph it says something about the attack on the village of Recani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was taking place on the 31st of March, 1999, that is to say six days after the bombing started.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Self-evidently we know nothing about the provenance of this document, and I -- we don't have a translation either, but before we can really go any further in considering these documents, the Prosecution would need to know what is going to be said about its provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The index of this tab 138 says it is written papers of KLA members. But this is not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the whole thing is a mystery to me. And of course in this considerable body of material, or for this considerable body of material I have to decide what parts of it to deal with at all, and if so, how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And from the next page on it is 1998. So this page is inserted by some mistake, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Inserted in some way, certainly. And I haven't yet seen any report or other document that produces any of this material. It's simply the words of this witness. So in making my decision as to which parts of the material to respond to, I am always assisted by knowing what's the best available evidence of its provenance, and at the moment for this particular document none and for the rest of this tab very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the first thing, there's no translation. I'd like the document to be placed on the ELMO. And secondly, I'd like evidence relating to its provenance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'll ask the witness straight away. I'll ask him to tell us whether he knows anything about where the document came from. However, this entire written text which has been cut off with this document and then carries on talks about intensive activity on the part of the KLA throughout the time this diary was kept, which means that it spans a period in 1998, and without a doubt since it was seized at that time it cannot contain documents dated 1999. But it does show how the KLA worked, how it came by its weapons, how it attacked the security organs at the border crossing, what their aim was, how they were deployed, and so on and so forth. Now, let's try and establish where this document came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The document spans a period in 1998. The Chamber has already ruled that we'll not hear any more evidence at this stage in relation to 1998. So we'll hear no evidence on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Unless it relates to 1999. It seems to be unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm going to ask you just to take a look at something that was written in handwriting on the document, although it does indeed refer to 1998, because in document 31/436, we see that it speaks about the constitution and functioning of the executive organ of the local staff of the KLA for Prizren and it says how the units were formed, were established. And we can see, for example, that an execution platoon was being established, execution squad, and a unit for abductions and kidnappings. So what it says -- assassinations and kidnappings, in fact, and then it says what followed. So if in 1998 they established squads for execution and units for kidnapping and assassinations and all the rest of it that it says here, and you can read it and find it in handwriting on the document, then I assume it's clear what these people were about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bonomy and myself are trying to find the document. The documents are not in any particular order, and it's very difficult to find them. You must wait until we have found the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Top right-hand corner number as you go through the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What -- the difficulty we have is in B/C/S there's only one page, but there's a substantial content in English version.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that you are looking at the English version. On 31-346/98.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, General?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a prison police under C that they were establishing?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the following page is there reference to units that will be established for assassinations and kidnappings?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that is the following document, the next document, 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it says "Execution Squad" under number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says: "All of this with the approval of the commander and the Chief of Operations of the local staff of the KLA."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what I'd asked you was to explain the source, the provenance of the document which is now on the ELMO and which has the heading 31.03.1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the previous document that had to do with the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain the provenance of this document 12-115, the one that you quoted a few moments ago, the attack on the village of Muhovljani and the village of Recani, where they torched a few houses, made the Serbs suffer great losses, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that, but I'll try to be even more specific. There is no doubt that this entire material was found in the village of Leskovac near Prizren after a particular action, and there is no doubt that it is included in the official archives documents of the Ministry of the Interior. Of course, this document, 12-115/99, deviates a bit from what I said just now because it bears the number 99 and 115. Possibly it got into this bundle by accident. It, rather, belongs to a different set of documents, because I see all the other documents have the number 346/98. So I cannot say anything specific about this detail, but I'm sure that this document is also part of the official documentation of the Ministry of the Interior; otherwise, it would not have been here and it would not have borne such a number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- registered and happened.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that what they found here as a document was verified from a factual point of view, and was it found to correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is simply putting words into the witness's mouth. While I'm on my feet, let us deal with this evidence a little more generally. First, yet again the point can be made, and it must be made: All this material should have been provided in advance with a report and it would have been possible for our people to have taken time out of court to read it and consider it. If that had been done, we wouldn't be spending an enormous amount of time on this document of uncertain provenance that we're dealing with now. Second, if the accused wants to produce evidence like this, which is secondhand, or it may be thirdhand in the sense that this witness only produces it, he's got to be able to lay a proper foundation so that all of us can know what, if any, weight to attach to it. I'm in no position at the moment to take a view one way or another about any of this material. And if I don't know more about its provenance, I may never be able to do so. So I would invite the accused, through directions of the Chamber, to be more disciplined in his approach to this material, and possibly, if he's going to carry on with documents of this kind through other witnesses, to reconsider the appropriateness of preparation by reports and by getting people to read this material in advance. It will save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're dealing with the provenance of the document on the ELMO. When you come to cross-examine, Mr. Nice, you may have one or two questions and then it will be a matter for the Chamber to determine what weight, if any, to attach to this evidence. That's the way the matter will be dealt with. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I don't know what can be called secondhand or thirdhand evidence, but there is no doubt that this is handwritten, that these were notes in Albanian that were seized, as it says in the document, and it has to do with the series of terrorist actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's move on to another area of the evidence relating to 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I certainly don't have a handwritten copy of a document written in 1999. And the witness himself says he doesn't. He has simply a Serbian translation of the document, as I understand it. So we don't have the original, and there's no point in spending any more time on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm just dealing with the handwriting, and we are going to establish where this one page comes from, how come this one particular page got into this set of documents. Tab 138 contains the translation of this entire handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say tab 138 is a translation of the document which is now on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The witness explained that the document on the overhead projector - as far as I can see, it's the one that bears the number 31/99 - is a translation of the document that got in from another set of documents. And as I look at it myself, as I go Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. through these voluminous documents, this document cuts through. It doesn't belong to it logically or physically. We are going to establish where it comes from, from which exhibit. I've been dealing with tab 138, which has a copy and a translation of the document that I quoted. The execution squad, the unit for abductions, different combat units, all of that is contained in the handwritten note, everything that was quoted, except for this one particular piece of paper that has to do with the attacks on Muhovljani and Recani. All the rest is contained precisely in this document, everything that was quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you're taking us now to 138. What tab in 138? Mr. Milosevic, if the Chamber decides to exclude this evidence, there is nobody to blame but yourself, because the evidence is not being presented in a proper fashion. Where are you taking us to now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I really don't know how to present this properly. If I give you a photocopy of a handwritten document that was found and seized by the KLA, if I give you a Serbian translation, and if I give you an English translation of the handwritten note and the information where the handwritten note was found and when and under what circumstances, I don't know how else I can deal with it, how else I can present it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me understand the organisation again. The handwritten part is written in Albanian. Is that right, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Excuse me: For the most part. Perhaps there are a few pages that are typewritten in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And that part is followed by Serbian translation, which is typed in Cyrillic letters and which has the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But among them, this 12-115 was put in by accident. This is not a part of the document. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously it doesn't belong to this set of documents because these documents from this voluminous case all bear the number 346 after the actual page numbers. This document has 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will not spend any more time here. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, as for the consequences of what is contained in this document in tab 138 and this organisation, what could you establish? When I say "organisation," I'm referring to these armed groups, say about 40 men, the organisation of executions, abductions, et cetera. What did you personally establish in Kosovo and Metohija in view of everything that is contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that with regard to these quotations from the text coming from this voluminous material that this corroborates some of the things I stated yesterday in response to many questions. They actually confirm the tables that we analysed and that show that the consequences of terrorist attacks were greater for the civilian population than the members of the police. Some parts of the text quoted today from this material is -- can also be linked up to one of my answers given to one of the questions put yesterday; namely, that civilians are leaving villages after armed conflicts. Of course, in the groups of civilians, the villages were left by the terrorists, too, who had been fighting before that, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, I'm stopping you because we have that evidence already. We have that evidence already. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, just tell us, in conclusion as regards this particular subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I said move on to another area. That area has been exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please take a look at tab 142. What does tab 142 contain?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 142 contains a particular information on operations carried out in order to curb terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija. The date cannot be seen, but I hope that it will be ascertained from some part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this a document of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that document, is there an indication of terrorist attacks and their consequences?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is under I in page 1 -- on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is 1998 again. We're not dealing with that now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're looking at it from the point of view of the police. Before we looked at it from the point of view of the KLA. It needs to be looked at from both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I had instructed you to move on. If we -- if the Chamber finds it necessary, we'll allow you to return to 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you wish to address the Chamber, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did wish to, Mr. Robinson, in relation to what you decided, not to deal with 1998 at this point in time. I just wanted to ask you to accept one exception, two points that correspond directly to the answers given by the witness that had to do with civilians, nothing else. I'm going to skip over everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You wish to put two questions to the witness. Very well, two questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 3, there is a paragraph that says: "Attitude towards civilians in combat actions. When carrying out actions, members of the Ministry of the Interior engage targets selectively. Only those where Albanian terrorist gangs were attacking from. They took care to protect the civilians as much as possible and in cases where the Albanian terrorists placed women and children in front of them as a human shield members of the ministry abstained from firing. The Albanian terrorists generally took advantage of this and fired all their weapons from well fortified ramparts and rifle slits that surrounded their houses and villages." As regards their attitude towards civilians, does this fully reflect what you had said?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. What you've read out just now fully corroborates my answers to previously put questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Another question related to this pertains to a chapter two pages later: "Activities related to the return of civilians to their villages and towns." Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to quote very briefly. "Inhabitants who fled due to terrorist attacks are now returning to their homes and daily chores. The Albanian population that moved temporarily to quieter areas of the province and towns after the terrorists expelled them, are returning to their homes. Several thousand refugees are returning to their villages to which sufficient quantities of food have been supplied by members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and in which they are guaranteed a quiet life and safety." Then the number of citizens returning to their homes are referred to or, rather, the number of those who have already returned home at the time when this document was compiled. General, does everything contained in this document correspond fully to what you testified about in relation to the consequences of terrorist attacks, the consequences in terms of the civilians and, generally speaking, the position of civilians throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nice I anticipate will be objecting. That is -- that's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While I'm on my feet, this is another document, and I must raise these matters as they turn up because it would be unrealistic to cover it in cross-examination where we've got, I think, 4, 5, 600 documents possibly to look at. As to this document, there is no indication apart from the 15 - possibly 13.1 - on the top right-hand corner of the front page written in hand of its date, of its precise provenance, of its author, or of to whom it was addressed, and if the accused wants to leave it like that or if the accused does leave it like that, then I almost certainly won't be able to deal with it and will simply have to invite the Chamber to set it at naught in due course. It's a matter for the accused, but the Chamber may think that it would be helpful to know more about documents like this than the bear fact of their production as part of the Defence exhibit binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If the assistant minister of the interior tells you it's a document from the Ministry of the Interior, is that not something to which weight is going to be given in assessing the position and is it not a matter for you to cross-examine about when it comes your turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course that's -- both of those are possibilities. The problem with that is that my ability to prepare for this is substantially different in the circumstances Your Honour outlines and in the position we find ourselves than if, for example, the witness says this was part of a report prepared at the request of so-and-so for so-and-so, whatever it is, because then I can start the process of deciding whether, and if so how, to investigate the matter to check on what requests we may have made for such documents to which no responses have been made in the past and so on, but if it just comes in the bear form, there's very little I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with you entirely that all of this evidence could have been presented with a covering note from the ministry certifying the position and explaining what all these documents were. It could have been presented in five minutes here and dealt with properly with time out of court, and we're being faced with a -- with a ridiculous situation which is not at all working to the benefit of the accused in the conduct and use of his time. I want to ask one question of the witness also in relation to this document that we're looking at. Does it anywhere, Mr. Stevanovic, contain information about the number of Albanian terrorists or Albanian civilians who were killed in the operations which are described here as operations to crush the Albanian terrorists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Bonomy, I would need some time to be able to establish whether this particular report contains that information, but it would be logical to find it here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, on -- already on page 1 we have references to terrorist attacks, and in paragraph 2 of this chapter headed "Terrorist attacks and consequences," it says that a total of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so-and-so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question relates to the consequences for Albanians. I see that there's plenty of information about the consequences for the Ministry of the Interior staff, but what I want to know is when you're preparing a report which is all about operations aimed at eradicating terrorist activities, do you not at least try to assess success of these operations by putting in numbers of people killed, whether they were terrorists or civilians? And I'm trying to find that in the document and I was looking for assistance from the assistant minister for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Certainly, Mr. Bonomy. Of course. I will help you find it in this document. Already on page 1 -- I was not able to read through it in great detail, but I know what the truth is. On page 1, and let me draw your attention to the fact that this document speaks about citizens -- civilians, but it also specifies their ethnic background. So in this chapter "Terrorist attacks and consequences," it says in paragraph 2: "Abducted: 156 Serbs and Montenegrins, 42 Albanians, 9 Roma, et cetera." Two paragraphs below, it says: "102 terrorist attacks were carried out against citizens and other facilities in which 74 citizens were killed out of whom 10 Serbs and Montenegrins, 29 Albanians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a section dealing with this which is headed "Consequences for the enemy," and it's a simple matter and it seems to me there is no reference to the numbers killed. You'll see the -- there's even a sentence -- I was trying to test the witness's familiarity with the document, but there's even a sentence in the document that says, "The Albanian terrorist began had about - blank space - killed and numerous wounded." Now, is that it? There's nothing more in this document about the consequences for the terrorists, apart from the fact that some were -- there are details of those that were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely in this chapter, Your Honour, we can see some of those consequences for KLA members. I cannot find a number that would designate the number of those killed, but we can see figures reflecting measures taken against members of terrorist gangs. It says, among other things, from the 1st of January to the 29th September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question that it doesn't tell us how many terrorists were killed and how many Albanian civilians who might have been human shields or collaborators were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until this moment, I haven't managed to find this figure here, which of course doesn't mean that there either weren't or were civilians and terrorists who were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is some information about people detained, 244 detained. It's in the second paragraph. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But let's move on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I had given you permission to ask two questions. We have to move on now. Those questions have been asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, we have just gone through certain topics that reflect intensive violence. Since you spent rather a long time in Kosovo, can you tell us whether the use of weapons was preceded by a period when members of the separatist movement tried to achieve their goals by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is common knowledge that before they began to use violence to attain their objectives, members of the separatist movement did not try to achieve these goals by peaceful political means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which way did they avoid political and peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is also well known that they boycotted the work of state and other organs. And what is even more important, they ignored and boycotted parliamentary and other elections in the Republic of Serbia for many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to establish if this phenomenon of boycott was represented in one, several, or all cases as expulsion of Albanians from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... unless I'm mistaken, we have had evidence on this particular issue already, boycotting and the general attitude of the separatists. Move on to another topic, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you commented yesterday on a whole series of tables showing how violence escalated, in which periods, and what it looked like in the period just before the war, during the war, and after the war, that is after our forces withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija. I would like to ask you now: What did the events after the arrival of international forces show? And those things that happened that you have information on, do they support --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the theory of Albanian separatists that the aim of their struggle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you appear to be reaching that stage in your examination-in-chief where diminishing returns are setting in. I will not allow that question. It is repetitive. There is no need to manufacture questions. The witness has been -- has been here for over two days, three days. If you have no more questions, we'll conclude the examination-in-chief and Mr. Nice will begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many more questions, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will be allowed to ask them if they are relevant, if they are not repetitive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. That's very kind of you indeed. I will now ask the witness to open tab 108. This is a very informative, I would say, analysis, a very edifying one. On the first page we read September 1999, Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, public security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do not appear to have a translation of this, and it's a long document, running to 20-odd or 30 pages. Was this submitted for translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. It was submitted for translation. It seems that you haven't got that translation yet. But if you agree, I can go through certain parts of this document. The witness will speak to them and you will receive the translation eventually if you think that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, it seems to be dealing with the events in 1998, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was done in September 1999, and it deals with the terrorism by Albanian separatists in Kosovo and Metohija and their methods. And I suppose it also refers to 1998, but it includes information up to and including September 1999. You have seen a lot of information related to that period, and I will not stop to deal with any particular piece of information, but this is an extremely useful document for understanding terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the document is not translated. We already have enough evidence relating to 1998. If you can point us to areas of the document that relate to the indictment or, more specifically, to 1999, then we can have those areas placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, already on the first page of the text, which is after the cover page, we see the contents, and I can note -- that is, the document notes that terrorism escalated in the second half of 1998 and the beginning of 1999 with cruel murders, killings, and assassinations of men, women, and children on their doorstep. And it also says MUP members were killed perfidiously, usually from ambush, while they were going about their regular duties. It deals later with the escalation, noting the fact that there were 14 times more attacks in 1998 than in the entire previous seven-year period. And then after the KFOR arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, by this time it is possible to detect a pattern in the way you present your Defence. You're charged by the Prosecution with the commission of certain acts. In relation to Kosovo, the precise date is January 1999 to June 20th, I think, 1999. But you have a passion for evidence that relates not to that period but to the period leading up to it. I have said that that may not be irrelevant to the extent that you may be seeking to show a pattern, but you must come to the charges in the indictment. The Chamber will not allow you in perpetuity to lead evidence in 1998 unless you have some evidence relating to 1999, because that is the only way in which it becomes relevant. It would then lead one to believe, if you are not going to deal with 1999, that your purpose is not forensic. So what we want here is to find evidence, if you have any, that relates to the allegations in the indictment touching upon the relevant dates that I have identified. Otherwise, the exercise becomes non-forensic and appears to serve some other purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, when I present a document as it was written, as it stood in the original, you must bear in mind the fact that none of these documents were compiled with a view to anything regarding what you call the indictment. They are just official documents written by the authorities from the times that they relate to. The one that you have before you on the table now states quite clearly in the period from the 1st of January, 1998, until the 28th of September, 1999. So the date is clearly stated, and it is a period of time which incorporates 1998 and in and including September -- 28th of September, 1999, when the document was compiled. Now, I cannot think up an artificial cut-off date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Very well, Mr. Milosevic. Take us to the relevant areas in the document, bearing in mind that it is not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I ought to make clear my reservations about hearing further general evidence about the conduct of KLA terrorists rather than hearing evidence about the specific incidents which are referred to in the indictment. It would appear to me to be relevant to look at this document if it deals with incidents which are features of the indictment or behaviour during the period of January to June 1999, which is referred to in the indictment. And short of that, the document appears to me to be repetitive of material we've already heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Take us to the relevant areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll indicate the relevant material, but you insisted on 1999, and I fully respect that. However, I'm quoting point 17, which says that this joint criminal enterprise occurred in October 1998 at the latest and went on throughout the period that crimes -- when the crimes alleged in counts 1 to 5 of this indictment occurred, beginning on or about the 1st of January, 1999. So there's reference to joint criminal enterprise here and the functioning of the state. And you speak of the functioning of the state and its attempts to defend themselves from terrorism. You refer to that as joint criminal enterprise, and that's the crux of what we're discussing here. I cannot bring evidence to show who hit whom with -- and whose hand hit somebody and how that somebody fell and things like that. What I can talk about is what I'm doing, that what is stated here is that the police committed crimes, whereas here we have a very competent witness, a police general, with 500 documents brought with him, testifying to the conduct of the police, what orders the police received, what the police did, and whether that can in any way be claimed to be what is alleged here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't want a speech. I've already told you to take us to the relevant areas of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, please, would you set aside or do you want me to quote portions from this document?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could be of assistance if I were to say that this is an official analysis conducted by the Ministry of the Interior which incorporates both 1998, but of course the entire period of 1999 up until the date that is stipulated, September, if I remember correctly. September 1999. So it refers for the most part to that period of time, but of course it does deal with the period that goes before and the period after the war as well. Some of the facts stated here have already been presented at the previous sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To shorten matters, on page 3 it says that up until September 1999, 5.527 terrorist acts were carried out.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say how many persons were killed, and that number is 945 persons, 654 citizens. So 654 citizens of which 291 Serbs and Montenegrins, 243 Albanians, and 19 members of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these -- are these different statistics from the ones we have already had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they aren't different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They should be the same.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, this is just an analysis which deals with the same facts and information. So the figures cannot be different, but it supplies exact information as to what happened and how, and that is why it is very useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the point? We've heard it already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is that since this is a comprehensive analysis, that it be admitted into evidence, because if you read everything it says in that document, then of course what is -- what you're trying to explain as some kind of criminal enterprise against Albanians would be completely nonsensical. And it's not only this analysis that bears that out but other documents as well, because what is stated here is not founded upon any evidence whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic, if there is any part of the document that relates to the period January to June 1999 and that relates to allegations in the indictment, we'll hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked, since it is a comprehensive document of the Ministry of the Interior, to be admitted into evidence. I'd like to tender it. I'm not going to quote it any more, quote from it any more. We have presented the relevant data with respect to terrorist attacks and we analysed them in detail yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously as to other exhibits there may be need to argue the position later, but if that's the limit of evidence the accused brings for this document that is not translated and is not available for us to read, I'd ask the Chamber to rule here and now that it is not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what we have said is that we'll consider this at the end of the -- end of the evidence, all questions relating to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the next area of your evidence, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the witness what he knows about the attacks carried out on religious sites, cultural monuments, schools, health centres, humanitarian workers, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, answers to that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that relate to any specific charge in the indictment? And if so, please direct us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's all in one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please direct us to the paragraph in the indictment to which it relates.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll get to the paragraphs in the indictment, but what we're discussing here is a general situation, a general situation in which the police acted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are not discussing a general situation. This is a trial. You're charged with specific charges, and your evidence must relate to those charges. In a way I'm glad you said that, because it shows that you're moving in the wrong direction. It's not a general situation. You are not at large. You must bring evidence that is relevant to the charges in the indictment, and I will not allow evidence unless it relates to specific charges in the indictment or to specific paragraphs, because we are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you have -- if you have a non-forensic purpose in mind, this is not the platform for it. Evidence about attacks on religious sites, cultural monuments, schools, may be relevant, but the evidence must relate to the indictment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you've just said that I am charged with concrete counts. Could you tell me which concrete act contained in the indictment it is that I committed and whether it is in there, because they, too, say that it doesn't exist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have -- I have stopped you. I have stopped you. The indictment was read to you at the beginning of this trial, and you are familiar with it. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not as clever to be able to know which act it was that I committed since you have to tell. Otherwise, I think it's time for the break, so I suggest that if you have nothing against that, we go ahead with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have passed the time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, we heard here as a witness Paddy Ashdown, British politician. In tab 40, you will find a brief extract from the transcript of that testimony. I'm going to quote from it briefly. I'm going to read out a portion of what he said, and then I'm going to ask you to respond or, rather, to answer my question. It is on page 27 of 84 pages of the testimony of Paddy Ashdown. Towards the bottom of the page he says the following in answer to my question. My question had to do with that it was a well-known fact that they were terrorists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 40 is a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's not tab 40.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 140.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I made a slip of the tongue, maybe I wasn't heard properly; I'm talking about tab 140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is not an authentic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was what I was given. It says ICTY at the top, Friday, the 15th of March, page 27 of 84. I assume the daily record or transcript, the LiveNote. May I be allowed to continue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this does not appear to be the transcript of the evidence. Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked my associates to extract this from the transcript of the testimony of Paddy Ashdown. So I assume that is what they did, that they took it from the transcript that we have here. I don't know where else they could have got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In case it's of any assistance, on the version of LiveNote that I have, this part of the evidence starts at the foot of page 2398, and the -- I'm looking at the very first full question: "Please show both -- please show both. You can see here both -- both the charts and also the consequences involved." That's word-for-word the same that appears on the LiveNote transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So we can readily enough check the accuracy of what seems to have been taken off a website against the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. Milosevic, proceed. If there is any inaccuracy, we'll be able to check it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The answer of Mr. Ashdown reads as follows: "[In English] Mr. Milosevic, I never denied that it was a terrorist organisation. I have never in any sense sought to excuse the suffering, the pain, the murder of innocent Serbs or Serb civilians by this organisation. I took steps, indeed, to make recommendations as to how that could be ended. I have never denied, either in my evidence or so far as I know in any other speeches or articles that I've written, that there was KLA activity, that innocent Serbs were suffering. But none of this, none of it justifies or excuses the use of excessive, outrageous force by your armed forces under your control in an indiscriminate, punitive manner, across the whole of civilian population in direct --" That's -- [Interpretation] And so on. There's a dash in the transcript. So I hope that that completely coincides with the transcript that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, General, Paddy Ashdown, as you've heard, said that he never denied that it was a case of a terrorist organisation but that here they were -- there was the use of excessive force. Now, we're going to deal with some questions which give an answer to whether it was in fact use of excessive force or not. But before I go on to that, I'd like you to tell me, what you think about this observation made by witness Paddy Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is rather a lengthy observation. I think I have understood it correctly. I can absolutely agree with two points that he made in his assertion, Mr. Paddy Ashdown made. First, it is incontestable that it was a case of a terrorist organisation, the name of which was the KLA. And the second point is that I absolutely express regret for all the victims of the armed conflict, not only in Kosovo and Metohija and regardless of which side they were on. But of course I cannot agree with the observation that he made when he said that the police, generally speaking, as has been translated here excessive, outrageous and disproportionate perhaps to force. That is just not true. That, of course, does not mean that there were not individual cases where this was overstepped and that authorisation was abused in the application and use of weapons, of official weapons in the police force as a means of coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since this is an essential substantive question, so we're not challenging that it was an outrageous, that it was a terrorist organisation but that it was a case of excessive and outrageous force, how can you characterise the circumstances in which the police had to act in Kosovo and Metohija in this critical period of time, that is to say 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite obviously from everything I have said thus far, it is quite clear that the police in the second half of 1998 and the first half of 1999, that the police acted in highly complex situations in Kosovo and Metohija, and more specifically, they could be characterised by saying that there was an excessive supremacy of threats, that is to say that all the members of the police, and of course citizens, too, were under great threat, excessive threat from the KLA terrorist organisation as well as from airstrikes, NATO airstrikes, far above all the measures of the police and citizens of trying to protect themselves against threats of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's good that you referred to a particular statement by Mr. Paddy Ashdown, which I remember very well, because in my view that in large measure is the case against you and the case that you have to face. There's no contest that the KLA was an organisation involved inflicting pain and suffering and even murder. The question was the response and the excessive nature of the response. But you will not meet that charge by adducing evidence of the very general nature which the assistant minister is now giving. You will meet it by adducing evidence that relates to specific charges in the indictment. I have given you this advice before, and I know that your characteristic response is to suggest that I am saying that there is a burden on you, and I want to clarify that. The burden remains on the Prosecution. But to the extent that you are putting forward a Defence, my suggestion is that you concentrate the evidence on the specific charges. If the general is able to give evidence about any of these charges, and there are many in the indictment, that is what you should be doing, not leading evidence from the general where he gives his general impression about the KLA and about the conduct of Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand what you said, Mr. Robinson. However, you said at the very beginning that the question of this allegation and accusation of excessive use of force is a very important one. That is why I intend to put a few questions to the witness that give answers precisely to those allegations related to excessive use of force, questions that have to do with the working conditions of the police in Kosovo and Metohija, the way in which the police operated, the use of force by the police, and the legality of use of force by the police. I hope that you will agree that these are four subjects that have to be dealt with in order to have a clear picture as to whether there could have been excessive use of force and whether there was any excessive use of force. Because if you do not take into account the way in which the police operated, the use of force by the police, the legality of use of force by the police, I assume that you cannot reach an answer to that question, and I assume that that is what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, by what standard are you judging the legality of the use of force by the police? Whether the -- whether the police operated in a lawful manner is not judged by domestic standards. It will be judged by the standards pertinent to international humanitarian law, international criminal law. But the evidence which you say you will lead now is not irrelevant, but I do hope you will be able to -- you will be bringing evidence that relates to the specific charges. So let me hear the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the conditions of work of the police, and you said that these conditions were extremely difficult, and you explained that there were KLA attacks and that NATO was bombing and that that made the situation very difficult. Was that the core of your answer?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the core of my general answer, but of course I could say a few more words by way of detail, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As briefly as possible. The complexity of these conditions, in addition to what I've already said, was characterised by the fact that part of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was under KLA control to a degree. When the first NATO strikes came, there was quite a bit of confusion within all structures and at all levels. Also, roads could not really operate because of NATO threats. And as far as I know, the police and the military had to protect their own command posts by changing them very frequently. In addition to that, during the first days of NATO strikes in Kosovo and Metohija the main telephone exchange in Pristina was hit. This made it impossible to have efficient communication between the eastern and western parts of Kosovo and Metohija. All of this put together made it impossible for the police to function as it does in normal situations and keep under its control territories, settlements, and even its own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, when you say that the situation was very difficult, that the conditions were very difficult, already in tab 141 can we not see in what kind of conditions the police were operating in the field and what was going on? This is a dispatch --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This also relates to July 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 149, is there an order dated the 22nd of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, this is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since this has been translated, we have the opportunity to see -- would you please be so kind as to --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order for taking concrete anti-terrorist action. The date is the 22nd of May, 1999, but I think that we've already been through this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the involvement of MUP forces to act in concert with the army, and it's only from that point of view that we looked at this order. But now when we talk about the conditions of work, on the first page, when the enemy is described --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- is it established that on the 22nd of May, "Over the past 10 - 15 days, there has been an increase in the concentration and combat activities of the STS in the general Palatna region," and the other villages?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the kind of information usually contained in combat orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, "Ambushes and raids on individual vehicles and supply convoys have been intensified"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "The objective of the Siptar terrorist forces is to use surprise attacks to inflict troop and combat hardware losses, cause uncertainty among members of the VJ and MUP and hinder road traffic"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then there is reference to increased presence and concentration of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which areas and in which directions. All of this is on the 22nd of May, 1999. Then there is reference to weapons.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to standard infantry weapons, there are machine-guns that are referred to, semi-automatic machine-guns, hand-held rocket launchers, and 60 and 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says they have laid obstacles on the approaches to and inside populated areas by mining approach roads and abandoned houses. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all of that was done by the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says how they have been successfully inflicting casualties on the VJ and MUP, and then it says that their defence will probably be supported by NATO aircraft fire and cruise missiles from airspace.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of what has been described here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask, what's your connection with this document, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
