utterances.text: [Interpretation] My connection with this document is only based on the fact that it is contained in the documents of the Ministry of the Interior. Certainly according to this order, it is probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This wasn't issued to you as part of an order? This is just something that was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I then ask, Mr. Milosevic, what is the objective of the questions that are being asked at the moment? Assist me to identify what it is that this evidence will demonstrate that we haven't already had a great deal of evidence about from this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the question I just put, if you heard it, Mr. Bonomy. In what conditions did the police work at this critical point in time? And I read part of the order that has to do with action taken by the enemy side. I'm asking the witness, because he was in Kosovo and Metohija too, was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you trying -- are you accepting that the police acted brutally and are you trying to justify it with this evidence? I mean, what is it that is the relevance of the conditions under which the police were operating? Did they behave improperly because of these conditions or are you saying that they behaved properly? What is your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, my case is quite clear: En masse and generally the police behaved properly. Only exceptionally and individually some behaved improperly. Generally speaking, the behaviour of the police was in accordance with regulations and orders, whereas individuals did behave brutally but then were prosecuted by the same police. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why don't we get to the facts that show that? Why do we keep looking at orders about what should be done or what has been happening rather than get to the conduct of the officers themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I'm moving towards, that particular conduct, but it's necessary to find out in what conditions all of this was happening and whether it was possible in those conditions. You heard the witness's answer: Sometimes in these conditions it was not possible to keep each and every individual within the armed forces under control, even within the police force. And then in such conditions there is a greater likelihood of excessive behaviour. It does not justify excessive behaviour, but it describes what the police did in dealing with this excessive behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We dealt with tab 148, which is similar to this one. We can move on quickly. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under those circumstances, General, was it regular practice that Albanians would report to the police all the criminal acts committed against them by members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I omitted that important detail from my previous answer. Of course an important fact in relation to police conduct in that period is the fact that Albanians to a very large degree did not report security related incidents to the police, including the most serious ones. First and foremost out of fear from revenge, and also they were afraid to communicate with the police at all. That is certainly one of the reasons why the police could not record each and every incident and take action with regard to each and every incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In that situation, did the police try to use all means available to find out as much as possible with regard to all these incidents?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Even in the most difficult of circumstances, the police did its best to act the same way it acted in peacetime, as it usually does today, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we look at an example contained in tab 56. The date is the 23rd of May, 1999, Pristina. That is a dispatch, again the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 56. MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 156 you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I have the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The beginning of the last week in May, 1999. It's addressed to all the MUPs from 1 to 7, sent by the Staff. It says: "It is essential that you inform the directors of hospitals and other health care institutions to which killed and injured persons are taken that without exception and regardless of who they are (members of the MUP, the Yugoslav army, citizens) that they must immediately and without exception inform SUP duty operations services about this, and they will dispatch crime investigation inspectors to record basic details regarding these persons, the place, time, and manner in which the injury was caused and other details and submit them to the MUP staff." General, I asked you whether all available means were used in order to obtain information about any consequence that had to do with injured persons, killed persons without any discrimination whatsoever; citizens, MUP, army, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The police used all information possible to take measures within their jurisdiction. This has to do with my previous answer when I said that Albanians to a large extent did not report any incidents, including those resulting in loss of life. So the aim of this dispatch was probably to refer to a particular way of finding out about these incidents involving wounding, loss of life, et cetera, that is to say through health institutions where it is expected that these persons would be taken in first of all in order to receive treatment. The objective was, of course, to have as many such incidents as possible recorded so that the police could work on the further processing of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the police do any planning in advance when the danger of bombing was intimated? Did they consider how policework would be carried out in these new, different, difficult circumstances, and did they treat all citizens the same way from that point of view? I would like to draw your attention to tab 53, dated October 1998, and that has to do with measures and activities to prevent and remove any consequences in the event of NATO bombing of targets in Kosovo and Metohija. This was adopted by the staff of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, like any other state institution, has certain obligations in terms of preparations in case of aggression or of war. This document shows what the police planned to do in order to prepare for adequate reaction and adequate measures in a situation of aggression by NATO. It seemed quite certain at that time, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to B, during the bombing, referring to everyday bombing. And point 3 says: "Administer first aid to casualties immediately on the spot until it becomes --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Administer first aid to casualties immediately, secure socially owned and private property against looting and theft."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And take steps to clear roads and streets for normal traffic?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You can see that all these measures have to do with the period before the bombing, during the bombing, and after the bombing respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 55, dated the 18th of February, 1999, this document speaks of increased pressure and all the measures taken by the police to continue performing its duties under those new, difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This dispatch was written to notify the competent units of the ministry or, rather, to instruct them to take certain measures related to the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I note in the first paragraph a reference to significant movement of the population from the border areas towards the central areas. Would the witness be able to comment on that? Why would that have been anticipated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this particular segment is related to the logical assumption that in case of aggression by ground forces citizens from border areas generally tend to move towards the central territory, central part of the country, and this is just an assessment that this might happen. It doesn't relate, of course, to Kosovo and Metohija alone, it refers to all border areas of the republic. Because at that moment the aggression had not started yet, and all the information available to the police and the state authorities boiled down to assessments as to what might happen in case of aggression. Of course, a specific situation is always different from an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned that the police was working under aggravated circumstances in terms of possibilities for movement, communications, and every other way. How did the police act in those aggravated circumstances, especially when something would happen that you in your official terminology would call a security related event?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave a general answer to that question. I can only be more specific as to the sequence of steps that the police would take after receiving information about such an incident. So first, after receiving a report, the police would try to go out into the field to the site and check the accuracy of the report. If the report proves to be correct, the police would then take measures to secure the site and to inform the competent judicial organs. After that notification, the police would generally continue to act upon orders of those competent judicial authorities. That means they would perform an on-site investigation, with an investigative judge or alone but only if instructed to do so by the investigative judge. Also, the police would also conduct exhumations, perform certain logistical work related to post-mortems. They would also take steps to open a criminal forensic case file that is normally opened in every proceedings, especially judicial proceedings. And again upon orders of the investigative judge, they would assist in burying the dead persons who might have been killed in such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Tell me, in what situations was it impossible to document security related incidents?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Developing a file, developing the documentation of an incident would be impossible only if there was no report in the first place, when the police had no information about an incident, or in cases where it was impossible to find any trace of the incident that had been reported, so the police could not verify it, or the third possibility would be a situation when for security reasons it was impossible for the police to go on the site and check. Such cases in the time of the bombing were numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one question about the method of work of the police. We could understand from your previous answers what the key tasks of the police were, both in 1998 and in 1999. You have explained generally what the key tasks were. Now, did the police discriminate in any way on religious, ethnic or other grounds against any individuals or groups?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. The police undertook measures aimed solely against terrorists and criminals of any kind absolutely irrespective of their ethnic or other background. Their action was only dictated by the kind of acts committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how about the people they were protecting? Was there any discrimination there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The police took the same measures of protection for all persons regardless of their ethnic or other affiliation, only depending on the kind of threat they were under.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, what kind of measures did the police take in combatting terrorism in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've already spoken about this. Policework in this case can be divided into preventive work, reaction after terrorist acts, or planned action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the preventive measures?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gathering information about the activity and movement of terrorist organisations, protecting roads and population centres. In fact, preventive types of work were geared at not allowing incidents to happen, not allowing incidents that would make it impossible for the police to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any requests for protection from villages where an attack was expected and which you paid no attention to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly many such cases, especially at the lower level. I can recall one particular example where I myself went to the village. I think it was Istok village in the Crkolez municipality. It was a very small, purely Albanian village. The population was terrified and wanted to leave. But after we sent a small unit there and managed to convince them that they would be protected, they stayed, and I believe they still live in that small village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You told me that in other cases the police reacted and carried out anti-terrorist actions. What was more frequently the case, reaction to attacks or anti-terrorist attacks? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course more frequently the police reacted. Until July 1997, I believe, the police more frequently only reacted to attacks and tried to avoid the critical, high-risk roads and villages. In August and September the police undertook planned anti-terrorist actions, but even they, these anti-terrorist actions, were reactive in nature because they were a response to a series of attacks in various high-risk areas. In most cases the police only reacted to terrorist acts if such acts -- or, rather, the police reacted with prior notification to verifiers. However, in 1998, there were anti-terrorist actions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm interested in the -- let me wait for the transcript. I'm interested in the category of planned actions by the police. You just said that in most cases, even in relation to planned action, their action was reactive. But there must have been cases, I imagine, where planned action took place which could not be characterised as reactive. Would you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when I said that even planned anti-terrorist actions can be considered as a reaction, I explained the kind of reaction I meant as a response to a series of prior terrorist acts. Of course in such actions the planned element exceeds the reactive element, but it is again linked to action against specific groups in a specific area. So it can be explained as a reaction to the activity of such groups in certain periods. But mostly when planning is involved, it is an active operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the case of a planned action, if the police were to go to an area where they had information that the KLA was present, how would they conduct themselves? Would they engage the KLA first or would they wait on the KLA to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The goal of every anti-terrorist operation was to detect and arrest members of terrorist gangs, to bring them into custody. Every such action is preceded by the gathering of information and operative data about that group, its membership, the weapons they have, their bases, et cetera. When the operation begins, the police goes to the village in a unit of adequate numbers and structure depending on the resistance they expect. The police never opens fire first. The clearest difference between the police and the terrorists is, of course, that the terrorists' aim is to kill, and the police could not have had such an objective prior to the proclamation of the state of war or at any other time, for that matter. So the police goes towards that particular group, and they sometimes even know the names of the individuals, sometimes not. The police is authorised to use weapons as means of coercion in ways that are regulated by the laws and bylaws of the Republic of Serbia. Only undesirable consequences of the use of weapons as means of police coercion can be the death of a person, including a terrorist. The objective of the police is not to kill. Their objective is to detect and to detain. The aim of the terrorists, however, is to kill, from ambush usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can you give me an example of a planned action which would not be reactive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we were looking at one of the tabs - I can't remember which ones now - I think the number was 40, from 40 -- or, rather, 140 to 149, those tab numbers and the orders therein. So those orders speak about planned anti-terrorist operations, and each of them conditionally speaking can be termed active with the proviso that I explained and the caveat I made, that as such it had something to do with the previous activity and existence of specific terrorist groups, which can always be seen in point 1 of the order that we looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, to continue on from what Mr. Robinson was asking you, what is reactive and what is active, you mentioned the tabs, and in tab 149, for instance, in point 1, it says: "In the last 10 - 15 days there has been increased concentration and combat activity of the Siptar terrorist forces in the broader region around the village --" and then it says the villages.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So does that speak about the reactions in fact to the increased activities of the forces in the area?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Anti-terrorist activity would have no sense unless in the area there was a terrorist group and that the terrorist group was active and had been active in the previous period, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- engage in surprise action, surprise operations to inflict, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the question that I asked has been answered. Move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, did the police then work to secure documents on all security related issues?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all security related issues about which it had any knowledge whatsoever and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean independently of the circumstances, that is to say regardless of how the incident and event took place?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, irrespective of the circumstances. Just on the basis of the possibilities that were there, and I mentioned them in my response to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So independently of any affiliation on the part of the victim, the perpetrator, and so on?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, independently of who the victims were and who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, in tabs 76, 78, and 79, do we have a review of the security related events which resulted in death according to the dates as registered by the police on the basis of each individual case, the records the police kept for each individual case? Is that right? So take a look at those three tabs.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is tab 76 that I have in front of me. And there it is an overview of security related events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have a translation of tab 78, so can we use that tab 78?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kwon indicated to us that they have the translation of tab 78 and he asked whether that could be used, and since we have that translation, we might --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure isn't the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the document that we are addressing -- or, rather, document 78 is a schedule of registered crimes committed against Serbs and Montenegrins in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. And the previous one, number 77, is a summary of crimes against Albanians in the area of Kosovo and Metohija dating from the 1st of January until the 20th of June, 1999. 1st of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have had this before, Mr. Milosevic. We have had this before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those documents, Mr. Robinson, were dealt with when we had another witness here, Mr. Paponjak, I believe, so you're quite right, during the chief of the Secretariat of the Interior of Pec, Mr. Paponjak's testimony. But then that review, summary of crimes against Albanians and against Serbs, Montenegrins and the rest referred to the area of his Secretariat of the Interior, that is to say the territory of four municipalities covered by the Pec secretariat, whereas this summary and overview, which has an identical title and which we put forward when General Obrad Stevanovic testified, when this general testified, relates to the entire area of Kosovo and Metohija, and the information and facts there relate to the entire territory, but we didn't dwell on that during General Stevanovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. This relates to the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. You now have the possibility of seeing how one secretariat compiled this covering four municipalities and how this was done for the overall territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the area as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, as you heard, 76 and 77 are not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 77 is translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 77 is translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 77 and 78 have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please comment on those two, 77 and 78, then. 77 are crimes against Albanians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before he does that, just lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, is this an official document of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All the statistical data contained therein, are they based on concrete cases which the Ministry of the Interior has, the files it has?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you now please give us your comments on the summary we find in tab 77 and explain to us the methods used, what the vertical columns represent, what the horizontal columns represent.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do so, but I'd just like to mention that tab 76 is a better illustration of what we're discussing, although we can, of course, show that same thing using this tab. As we were saying, in tab 77, which is a statistical overview of the crimes committed against Albanians in the entire area of Kosovo and Metohija, the period is between the 1st of January, 1998, to the 20th of June, 1999, taken by the different periods of time. Yes, 77. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, if we look at the horizontal column, 1A, we are dealing with reported and registered crimes, as it says under 1A. Unfortunately, we don't have the total column, but we can add up. So the total number of registered crimes, reported and registered crimes in Kosovo and Metohija, with known perpetrators, the figure is 823; with unknown perpetrators, the figure is 2.603; and other, 136. Of course, if we look at the vertical columns you will be able to see the different periods. Column 3 is 1998; column 4 is up until the war, 1999; and column 5 is the wartime period of 1999. In A/2, the total number of reported and registered crimes has been broken up according to types of crimes and specific crimes committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we won't go into all the specific crimes committed, but what are the most characteristic points here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 125, which is terrorism. Of course, it is more important and -- to answer your question, what is on page 2, that is to say what the police undertook pursuant to the crimes committed. And if you look at page 2, for example, A3 of the horizontal column, we can see that a total of 1.563 on-site investigations were carried out by police pursuant to judge's authorisation. There were 1.240 of those; by the investigating judge, 287 is the figure there; by the investigating organs of the army of Yugoslavia, 8 cases of those; partially carried out investigations, 11; investigations not carried out, 1.014; forensic documentation was compiled for 804 cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, if you could tell me, what is Article 166?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Let me have a look. I'm not quite sure now, but we will find an explanation of the articles at the end of tab 78. 166 is theft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aggravated burglary or theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, when we say uncovering the perpetrators and throwing light on the case, we see that the number of perpetrators was 2.788, number of detected perpetrators of crimes, and that 2.623 were civilians, that the active police force numbered 36, the reserve police force came to 22, military personnel 2, active servicemen and from the reserve force, 105.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then we can see the number of criminal and other reports filed, 3.614 in the total. This whole table refers to crimes against Albanians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are there any other characteristic traits that you'd like to highlight here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there is anything that would be of special importance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the fact that it says that it was sent to the judiciary, judicial organs, the public prosecutor and the courts, and there were 3.691 of those, referred to the army 116, and others in progress, the number there is 465.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And tab 78 was compiled according to those same methods, except that in that case it is a summary of registered crimes committed against Serbs and Montenegrins and other non-Albanians in the area of Kosovo and Metohija from the period stipulated. Perhaps it is especially important for me to say that since there is no translation of tab 76, that of all these crimes committed, crimes resulting in death are to be found in tab 76. So that is especially important because of the consequences themselves. So that's tab 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, although the tab has not been translated, could you please indicate to us now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, tab 76, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there is no translation, I'm going to read out the title. It is a "Summary of security related events resulting in death that occurred in connection with armed conflicts in Kosovo and Metohija in the period from the 1st of January, 1998, to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1st of June, 2001 in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, broken up according to the periods of time." The structure of the table, vertically speaking, is also divided into periods, as I've already said, like the other ones, and I'd like to draw your attention to vertical column number 6, for example, because it relates to the period of the war. And now looking at it horizontally, point 1 is the number of events and number of persons that were killed. So the total number of events resulting in death during the war was 1.030, and for the entire period it is 1.879. The number of persons killed in these events during the war, we see 2.990, and a total of 4.419. Of course after that, we see the structure according to ethnicity. Albanians killed during the war or who lost their lives during the war is 1.614. The rest, 958 - I'm talking about the wartime period - and unknown ethnicities, there were 418 cases that resulted in death there. So in response to the question, I can say that the police just during the wartime period registered and recorded 1.030 events which resulted in death in which 2.990 persons were killed, and the police compiled the corresponding documents for those cases and took steps under its jurisdiction within the limits of its capabilities given the circumstances, the prevailing conditions. I considered that to be important. I wanted to tell you that. If need be, we can go on to analyse the table further, and it is a table comprising several pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very important survey and summary because it refers to the whole of Kosovo and Metohija. And as insistence here is on 1999, it stems from the 1st of January, 1999, and then we have the 23rd and the 24th of March, up until the 20th of June. And in the second chapter of the summary, we have the number of persons, ethnicity, sex, status, and so on. Now, status, when you have Albanians first.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. We have terrorists, civilians, members of the MUP, and unknown, according to their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Albanians, 1 member of the MUP died, that is to say one member of the MUP who was an Albanian who died, 538 terrorists, 700-odd civilians. That is during the war.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 539 and 783.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, does the list -- or do the statistics indicate the circumstances in which the various persons here mentioned were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they do include that, but let me take a look, because it should be found on one of the following pages. Yes. It's in point 3 on page 2. Number of persons killed per event and per national structure or ethnicity, and the first part of that table relates to terrorist attacks. So if you're able to follow, page 2, number 3, it says "terrorist attacks" in the column, vertical column, and then of the terrorist attacks there were 412 during the war, under 6; 567 under number 6, Albanians 43, others 524, unknown none. What it says here, if you can see it on the ELMO, relates to the anti-terrorist actions, ATA. The number of events 92, the number of casualties - and I'm just relating to the war period - 564; Albanians 517, others 42, unknown ethnicity 5. In the NATO bombing, the next column, the number of events was 156, the number of casualties was 617, of which Albanians 305, others 253, unknown ethnicity 59. In crimes, that is to say other crimes, the number of events during the war was 143, the number of casualties was 300 and -- or, rather, 328, of which Albanians 228, others 59, unknown 41. And other cases, miscellaneous, the number of events was 203, the number of casualties 914, of which 521 Albanians, others 80, unknown 313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you said these numbers only refer to the number of dead people; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Casualties being the deaths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that the title of the summary says a review of security related issues which resulted in death. So the title of that summary tells us that it refers to deaths, deaths incurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, these, then, are the facts and figures that the Ministry of the Interior has, and each of them, as you said, is based on a concrete case and case file, document, record, and so on that the Ministry of the Interior disposes of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you assess in the Ministry of the Interior whether the work of the police was effective and efficacious in Kosovo or not during the war?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessments and appraisals boiled down to the following: That it was commensurate to the conditions in which the police had to act. And all levels of leadership, all the leaders, in my personal opinion, according to my personal knowledge, did everything in their power to ensure that the police functioned under such difficult conditions to the maximum possible effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're coming up to the time for the break, and I want to raise a question of the length of this witness's testimony. You had scheduled him to testify for 12 hours. By the end of today, that time will have been reached. He will have been here for three days, and that's a little over 12 hours. When we return after the break, I'd like you to outline to the Chamber the structure for the rest of the examination, because we just received another 17 binders, which is an intimidating number in any circumstance, and I'd like you to give us an outline of the rest of the witness's evidence, and we intend to follow the rules quite strictly in terms of relevance of the evidence. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just give me an outline of the rest of the evidence that you wish to adduce. I want to get a time frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, in the best wish to use time as rationally as possible, to a maximum, I wish to point out that this witness, in view of the volume of his testimony, his competency, and the fact that many of these documents are an official nature, he will practically be worth ten witnesses or so, and I think that that is very rational use of time. As for the subjects I intend to deal with with this witness, the remaining topics, that is, that will briefly have to do with the degree of information from the MUP staff downwards towards Kosovo and Metohija upwards toward the ministry itself. Just a few questions in relation to that. Then I'm going to put some questions to him that have to do with the use of force by the police. You mentioned that the question was whether these standards that apply in my country differ from standards that apply in other countries. The questions will be very concrete. They will not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Let me -- not whether the standards in your country differ from standards in other countries but whether they are the same as the standards required by international law. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do hope that that goes without saying. Then, further on, questions that have to do with the legality of policework, then questions pertaining to incidents involving loss of death that are from this indictment, questions that have to do with the work of police involving incidents resulting in death and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Incidents mentioned in the indictment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But also incidents not mentioned in the indictment, in order to show the work involved. Then questions that have to do with clean-up and mop-up, mentioned here several times; crimes against personal dignity and morality and how they were treated. Rape cases were mentioned here, among others, and that belongs to that group of criminal acts. And then questions related to refugees, displaced persons. All of that has to do with allegations against Serb forces, as it is put here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What kind of evidence that is not of a very general nature can this witness give about rape, allegations of rape in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are some documents here. I cannot quote the exact tabs to you now, but there are some documents here that can indicate what kind of action police took with respect to these criminal offences. Yesterday, I showed you a document that had to do with the activities of the local police where an Albanian, a local policeman, reported the conduct of three persons in army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It is Article 7(3), responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further on, the alleged shellings of different facilities. The general will be able to give an explanation in that respect. Then questions related to paramilitary groups and volunteers, and some questions that have to do with the presence of MUP forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate it will take to conclude all these areas?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the examination on all these topics could be concluded during the first working day next week, and I won't be using all of it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those to which I personally attach the greatest importance would be the incidents resulting in death that are mentioned specifically in the indictment, the evidence on paramilitary groups and volunteers, and you said something about evidence relating to the movement of information upwards and downwards. That has to do with the line of command?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked about information going downward to the secretariat of the MUP in Kosovo and from the staff of the MUP towards ministry headquarters, vertically upwards, that chain of command. We have documents in these tabs about that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. So we expect to conclude in the first working day of next week. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, how did information flow down the chain from the staff of the MUP in Kosovo towards units in the field?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry staff provided daily information at least once a day to all subordinate units about everything that was going on in Kosovo and Metohija; namely, information that they considered important for the subordinate units. In the same way, the ministry staff issued specific orders to take specific measures regarding all questions belonging to the purview of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to that, in Pristina at the ministry staff, meetings were held every now and then with heads of the secretariats and the leaders of units sent to Kosovo and Metohija. At these meetings the security situation was analysed directly as well as the situation in the area, and specific assignments were given in relation to the situation. It was customary to draw up conclusions after every meeting, and then they would be sent on in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a few examples in terms of how this actually worked. For example, in tab 58, if you take a look at it, the ministry staff is addressing this to the chiefs of Secretariats of Internal Affairs, to the commanders and all persons concerned in Pristina, Prizren, Pec, Djakovica, Kosovska Mitrovica, Gnjilane and Urosevac. Then it says that all commanders of police stations are required to familiarise themselves with these dispatches. Is that the usual way of doing it?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one example of such a dispatch that was sent from the ministry staff to the Secretariats of the Interior and to the commanders of special police unit detachments. There are many more such detachments. They were the everyday form of communication between the staff and their subordinate units. It can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the regular everyday mode of communication. And in tab 59, you have information on the bodies found in the Kosovo and Metohija autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is topic-specific information that has to do with corpses found during a certain period of time in Kosovo and Metohija. Of course, it is not in the form of any order. This is an analytical presentation of what had happened in the previous period, namely, the corpses found in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does all of this have to do with bodies found as a result of activities carried out by terrorists?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at first glance I can conclude that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This has to do both with Serb and Albanian victims; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I note that this is October 1998. I am aware that the indictment does make allegations or, rather, contains certain charges which may be said to relate to this period, but only in a very general sense. The real body of the charges covers the period, as you know, January to June 1999. So when you're dealing with 1998, you have to justify it. What is the precise relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is to show how information flowed downward from the MUP staff to the secretariats and units in the field. If you think that these examples from 1998 are not sufficient, then, for example, in tab 61 you have 1999. That is the 26th of March. That is three days into NATO operations. A dispatch, an order of General Lukic to all the organs in the area, in Kosovo and Metohija, in tab 61. I hope you have this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not ignore what is in tab -- is it 58 or 59? What is the tab we are now dealing with, 59? Tab 59.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now dealing with tab 61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I was telling you that I will not ignore what is in tab 59, the one previously. Tab 61 now deals with 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It refers to the time at the very beginning of the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, can you see this? This is also a dispatch of the staff?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Obviously this is a dispatch of the staff of the ministry in Pristina, and the head of the staff is addressing this to his subordinates, the chiefs of secretariats and commands of all PJPs, measures that should be taken during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, can we just look at this passage where it says, "I hereby order, take the greatest effort to cover the area in order to detect and take measures against all perpetrators of the crimes," et cetera. And then para 2: "Prevent all crimes committed against persons of different ethnicity. Arrest perpetrators and file criminal reports."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Para 2, item 2, of this dispatch dated 26 March, it says: "Prevent all crimes committed against persons of different ethnicity. Arrest perpetrators and file criminal reports." This term literally sounds, in Serbian, "deprive of freedom," but it means to arrest. In para 3, I don't want to read everything. It says, among other things, strictly adhere to the Geneva Conventions regarding the civilian population and stock materiel and equipment in certain locations, et cetera. Is this one of the dispatches that was sent down to subordinate units particularly drawing their attention to these types of conduct that I quoted?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the typical method of issuing orders and instructions to subordinate units. Those subordinate units, in their turn, are expected to pass these orders on to the units directly subordinated to them so that the orders reach everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same dispatch received by teletype in another unit was -- is to be found under the next tab.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we just see a different type, depending on the communications equipment in various units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any way, we can see that this is received by all units.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then in tab 62, we find a dispatch dated 2nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. It is a similar dispatch, but this one is a copy of an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A copy of an original document that was sent on by teletype to subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This one has a signature, then. May I draw your attention to para 4 of this document, where it says: "All persons, regardless of the unit they belong to, which are found in the course of perpetrating the said serious criminal acts are to be arrested and turned over to civilian and military courts accompanied, by criminal reports, whereas criminal reports are to be filed to civilian and military prosecutors' offices, with prison sentences meted out to all such persons."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military and civilian courts, depending on the case, have jurisdiction according to the regulations we looked at in the previous days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Next we have another order issued by the Chief of Staff, dated the 6th May, which says: "In this connection in the following period take all measures to prevent paramilitary groups and individuals from committing violence, murders, rapes, and other criminal acts against the civilian population regardless of their ethnicity, any acts that would jeopardise the property or lives or other -- of civilians." This is the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab? You said tab 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 65. You must tell us the tabs. This is not a private dialogue between the witness and yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said tab 65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You did not. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here, along with this dispatch, there is a text -- the text of an article from the Politika newspaper, where it says in the beginning: "We are sending you an article from the daily newspaper Politika on the submission of reports to the president of the FRY by the head of staff of the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija, Major General Sreten Lukic, and the commander of the 3rd Army, Colonel General Nebojsa Pavkovic." This text ends with the words, "said the statement from the Supreme Command." General, what can we see from this press release?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I first say that this is a document issued by the staff in Pristina, which was made available to subordinate units in a way I described before. It is accompanied by the text of the press release published by -- after reports were made by Major General Sreten Lukic and Colonel General Nebojsa Pavkovic to the president. We see from this document that the entire personnel in the secretariat and all members of special police units must be familiarised with the text. In the next paragraph, attention is drawn to the necessity to prevent paramilitary formations and individuals from committing crimes against civilians, as you said in your previous question. This is another copy of an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It also says that in parallel with performing these defence tasks, numerous criminal acts involving violence, murders, rape, looting, et cetera, have to be controlled, and it also mentions the arrests of numerous criminals who posed a significant threat to the civilian population. Is that what is written in the press release?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it goes without saying that special attention should be paid to such conduct and appropriate measures taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The press release says: "In the interest of all the population of Kosovo and Metohija regardless of their ethnic and religious background." Is that what is written in the press release?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, at the very end of the newspaper article, it refers to a statement from the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, do you mean the last paragraph of this copied text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The very last words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A precondition for proper operation of public services and social functions of the state in the interest of all the population of Kosovo and Metohija regardless of their national affiliation." That is the last part of my text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The final English -- the final English words are "said the statement from the Supreme Command." Does that expression not appear in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. The last words are "said the statement from the Supreme Command." That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you understand by the expression "the Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Supreme Command is defined by the constitution of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, let me just try to avoid misunderstanding. This entire text is a press release by the Supreme Command, and it concludes with the words, "as reported by newspapers," and ends with the words, "according to the statement from the Supreme Command." This entire text is from the Supreme Command. And let me just point out one passage where it says that in Belgrade -- "In Belgrade, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Supreme Commander, Slobodan Milosevic, heard reports from the commander of the 3rd Army, Colonel General Nebojsa Pavkovic, and the commander of the staff of the police of the MUP of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija, Major General Sreten Lukic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would be grateful not to be interrupted when I'm asking questions of a witness. What do you understand by the Supreme Command that would issue such a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me be very specific: We in the police were not concerned with form. What was most important for us was what positions were taken and what policies were adopted, and the policy was to enforce the regulations lawfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the answer that you don't know? Or do you have an answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question you asked, Mr. Bonomy. I don't know if the witness understood it properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question was very simple. Please carry on with your own examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, it seems to follow from this that the witness does not know what "Supreme Command" means, which should not be the case. He must know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can possibly clarify it in questioning him, but as far as I'm concerned, at the moment he's indicated he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say earlier, General, that the Supreme Command was established by law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said. In keeping with the constitution, I think my words were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you don't know who or what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do know. It is a body, but obviously I misunderstood the earlier question, because I thought I should explain in which way this press release was issued, who issued it, who drafted it. Of course I know what the Supreme Command is and how it operates. What I know is that the Supreme Command consists of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, presidents of member republics, and of course I know that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia issues orders based on the decisions of the Supreme Command. That is my understanding of this concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 73, General, we have another example of this communication, where it says: "At meetings held on the 7th and 11th May, 1999, at the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija with chiefs of Secretariats of the Interior and commanders of detachments of special police units, the following tasks were decided on and the following conclusions made." One of them is: "Ensure stability and security for everyone in the province, conduct sanitisation of the terrain with appropriate accompanying documentation." These are items --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are items 5 and 6. Thoroughly clear up the terrain and duly record it, in keeping with all prior orders. May I just add that these are conclusions from two previous meetings, and I'm sure that these conclusions were duly transmitted to all subordinate units for them to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Item 10 says prevent violence, killings, looting and other crimes and immediately issue a criminal report and bring in all people for whom there are grounds to suspect that they have committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Request the relevant judicial organs to expedite legal proceedings to the utmost in order to punish the perpetrators of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This refers to the way in which the police should work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says make sure that police officers carry out all said tasks lawfully, correctly, consistently and fully. Those responsible for this shall be chiefs of the SUP and detachment commanders.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 12 regards general crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are then --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are then specific measures that follow from the meetings held on the 7th and 11th of May, and they are listed here in proper sequence covering a number of areas, including item 16, which regards the conduct of the police including the wearing of uniforms, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And para 19 refers to the RPO.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reserve police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Members of reserve police units cannot wear police and military uniforms if they have not been mobilised and engaged in the reserve MUP or VJ formations."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why is this emphasised specially?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is specially emphasised because reserve police units were established to protect specific villages and towns, and as long as there is no specific danger, these persons should not wear uniforms unless they are mobilised by a concrete order. So these persons concerned are members of the reserve police force, but they have not yet been engaged in a specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, General, I think that we have spent enough time quoting examples and documents testifying to information from the staffs downwards, down the chain. Can we now take a look at how information was realised from the staffs of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo upwards towards the top of the ministry, up the chain. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the provisions governing information and information for the Ministry of the Interior, the staff informed the ministry, and the minister specifically, the heads of departments and from time to time the other assistants by way of daily reports, daily information, and urgent reports. Of course there were periodical reports as well that we were able to see when we discussed this issue earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you take a look at tab 60, please. It is a document dated the 1st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It has its number. There's no need for me to quote it. But can we see in this document precisely what you've said, that it was addressed to the ministry, the chief of public security, the public security department, the chief of the analytical administration, and so on.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a sample copy of a daily report which is titled "Summary of events, phenomena and information with a bearing on the security situation recorded between 0600 hours on the 30th of April to 0600 hours on the 1st of May, 1999." In this way the staff of the ministry would report on a daily basis to the headquarters of the ministry, or specifically the persons mentioned here, and from time to time other persons as well. The contents of this summary were compiled once again on the basis of daily reports coming into the staff from all the subordinate units over the past 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is information or the manner which information was sent up the chain.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a collective information or summary from 0600 hours on the 30th to 0600 on the 1st of May. And that's for a period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the type of daily information report that would be sent out?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is the -- what are the contents? The first paragraph deals with attacks of NATO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they describe what happened in the space of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 or, rather, point 2 refers to terrorist attacks, compiled according to the same methods. Then we come to point 3, serious crimes committed; point 4, persons who fled the territory of Kosovo and Metohija; and point 5, miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Point 4 is the longest portion, persons who fled the territory, and so on. Or, rather, single crimes are noted here, the crimes that were committed in the space of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And of course in this summary we can see the very different perpetrators, different types of perpetrators and the different damages incurred with the crimes perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have Serbs and Albanians there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And policemen, reserve policemen, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all of that is one information, one summary relating to a period of 24 hours; one day, that is.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, point 4 of this report, it says persons who fled the territory of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that on that particular day to which this summary refers, and it is the 30th of April, that at the border crossing of Djeneral Jankovic 4.764 persons left the area, of the Siptar ethnicity. Yes, that's right. And 11.400 persons belonging to the Siptar ethnic group left the territory via Vrbnica. Then we have, on April the 24th, a total leaving the country 715.158 of the Siptar ethnic minority, and it stipulates the border crossings they crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, was it customary and usual that this kind of summary report should provide an overview of all the important security related incidents and events?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All important security related events. They did not include events of lesser importance. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In relation to item 4, persons who fled the territory of Kosovo, there is no mention of the circumstances in which they fled. Wouldn't a report such as this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was asking whether a report such as this would comment on the circumstances giving rise to persons fleeing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the title of the report itself is a summary of important security related events. And you will see that on the previous pages they don't enter into an in-depth analysis of the events themselves, but they just set out the facts that a crime had been committed and then, in point 4, how many persons left crossing each of the border crossings. Of course, this is a question of method, of methodology. There could have been a comment accompanying this, but I assume that this was common knowledge from previous summaries of this same nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was common knowledge, generally known, do you mean that it was generally known and common knowledge why persons were fleeing Kosovo and Metohija? Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for those of us who were in the police force in Kosovo and Metohija, it was common knowledge to us why they were leaving, why they were leaving Kosovo and Metohija. We knew that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was generally known to you? What was common knowledge, your common knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew, generally speaking, that the trend of persons leaving their villages and homes had precipitously increased with the start of the aggression and the period that I said was a very difficult situation in which the police had to function, which was especially the period at the start of the aggression when, to all intents and purposes, there was general chaos, confusion. People were leaving, people didn't know what to do and all the problems that that gave rise to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now we're going to deal, as I said in the beginning in response to a question by Mr. Robinson, with issues that we're going to focus on briefly, and they are the use of force and firearms. General, the police along with the army was the only element of power and authority who had authorisation to apply force, to use force. Now, how was the use of force as you -- as used by the police prescribed?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right of the police to use force is one of the most sensitive rights that the police enjoy. In the Republic of Serbia, the manner in which vehicles of force are used, including official weapons, is regulated by the law governing internal affairs and the rules and regulations following that law and pursuant to that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly, what do the provisions say? I don't want to go back to all these provisions individually, but what were the general principles governing the use of force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the rules and regulations, we have clear-cut principles that emerge, and they could be explained in the following way: First of all, we're talking about the principle of the legitimacy of the goals. So firearms and every other means of coercion can be used only in cases which are prescribed in the law. After that, we come to the principle of graduality, the gradual application of the use of force, which means that an authorised person is duty-bound, when using force, to go from lighter weapons to more heavy weapons. And the third principle is the principle of necessity. And according to that principle and the provisions that prevailed it could be resorted to only when dictated by necessity, only when the need arose and when an assignment couldn't be carried out in any other way and the assignment was legitimate, of course. And the fourth principle was the principle of proportionality or, rather, a principle that implies that the force should be commensurate to the threat which that force is used to suppress.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, General. Now, all these principles in very precise ways are of course defined, but the ones you mentioned, are they to be found in the rules and regulations on the methods of the use of force which is a component part of tab 7?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They are to be found in those rules and regulations. They are not -- I did not quote them literally, of course, word-for-word, but the provisions contain what I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we need read out the rules and regulations and provisions. It is part of the evidence to be found in tab 7, so we won't waste time on that, but I assume that it is pursuant to the law governing internal affairs given in tab 1. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The important provisions governing of use of force is to be found laid out in the law and they are set out in detail in the supplement in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to draw your attention to the fact that we have the law governing internal affairs in tab 1, and in tab 7 the rules and regulations of -- on the use -- governing the use of force. We won't lose any more time in quoting the exact wording from those. But tell us, though, please, the leadership of the MUP, the leadership of the state, the local leaders as well, in practice, what was their attitude toward these provisions, the law governing internal affairs, for instance, and the rules and regulations for the use of force?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At all the important meetings that I attended and that I mentioned in part during my testimony, I personally gained the conviction that all the competent leaders insisted upon the fact that provisions governing the use of force, especially firearms, be followed to the letter. Not only in Kosovo and Metohija but generally in the whole country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, what about the weapons that were used by the terrorists when they attacked the police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrorists in their attacks on the police used all types of weaponry which they had at their disposal. That is to say rifles, anti-armour devices, anti-aircraft weapons, anti-tank mines, and everything else that they had at their disposal. And the consequences of the use of such devices are quite clear to one and all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now the police: From the very beginning, was it capable of responding in adequate terms to conduct of the terrorists in this way, and did they -- were they able to match those weapons?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of 1998, the police was not able to do that, principally because the terrorists chose their location, the target of their attack and the place of their attack, and as we said, their goals were to kill, and therefore they used ambush and brutal attacks on the police and the citizens while they were moving along the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the police forced to use protective devices and weapons which matched the weapons used by the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The police was forced to change the type of weapons it used and to include those protective devices that could adequately -- and other weapons that could adequately respond to the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have one question now, and I'm sure that you're professional enough to answer it because I'm not quite clear on this point. For example, the police had an armoured transporter, APC; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the terrorists did not. They didn't have an APC?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So would you say that the police was using heavier weaponry than used by the terrorists in that case?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the police had the APCs as a protection device, a protection vehicle, because the APCs have incorporated into them weapons, but the weapons on an APC cannot, of course, prevent terrorists waiting in ambush and opening fire against an armoured device like an APC from a hand-held rocket launcher, for example, or a recoilless gun or anything like that, even using ordinary more sophisticated weapons. Among other things, we found certain rockets produced, the Armbrust type produced by Germany, modern weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, as far as calibre is concerned, what was the calibre on an APC? What does an APC have, for example?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An APC has an anti-aircraft machine gun 12.7 millimetres, or sometimes 14.5 millimetres in exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is practically the same calibre that we were able to see, according to the list, that the members of the KLA had?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely identical, yes. With the proviso that the calibres that the terrorists had against an armoured device were bigger and different, and the intention was different, of course; the purpose of it was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just take a moment to look through this. Can you explain to us, please, what we find in tab 143, for instance, where there is a dispatch, a telegram by the staff of the MUP to the ministry in Pristina, where it says that plan, organise and undertake actions from a distance targeting terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but what tab number did you give us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
